title: WaveFreqAnchor: Wave-Structural Anchoring and Frequency Correction Diffusion for Training-Free Face Restoration

paper.title: WaveFreqAnchor: Wave-Structural Anchoring and Frequency Correction Diffusion for Training-Free Face Restoration
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion-based face restoration that adjusts the sampling trajectory of pre-trained diffusion models has achieved remarkable progress. However, existing approaches provide insufficient constraints during reverse diffusion, causing identity-related structural drift and degraded fidelity under severe degradations. To address this, we propose WaveFreqAnchor, a training-free framework based on Wave-Structural Anchoring and Frequency Correction Diffusion. Specifically, Anchor-Space Wave-Structural Guidance (ASWG) constrains facial structures through anisotropic wave-response consistency, while Multi-scale Wavelet-Fourier Injection (MWFI) aligns the predicted low-frequency subband with the observation by replacing its phase, correcting inconsistencies accumulated during reverse diffusion. For real-world scenes, we further introduce Subband High-Frequency Enhancement (SHE), which performs bounded, spatially masked refinement on the predicted high-frequency subbands to recover fine facial details under unknown compound degradations. Together, these designs effectively preserve facial identity while restoring sharp and realistic facial details. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving high-quality and high-fidelity face restoration.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Overview of our WaveFreqAnchor. Given the input observation, ASWG provides gradient guidance for posterior sampling, while MWFI corrects the predicted low-frequency wavelet subband using the observed phase and preserves the high-frequency subbands from the guided update. For real-world inputs with missing high-frequency details, SHE further refines the predicted high-frequency subbands before the posterior update. Face restoration ( Li et al. 2025a ) aims to recover a high-quality face image from a degraded input. Under severe degradations, only coarse facial structures and limited identity cues remain, making the restoration problem highly ill-posed and often leading to plausible yet identity-inconsistent results. Existing methods leverage generative facial priors ( Wang et al. 2021 ) , discrete codebooks ( Zhou et al. 2022 ) , and diffusion priors ( Lin et al. 2024 ; Wang et al. 2025 ) to constrain the solution space. However, even when producing visually realistic results, they often fail to faithfully preserve the observed facial structures under severe degradations. Achieving both realistic detail synthesis and structural fidelity therefore remains a fundamental challenge. Pre-trained diffusion models ( Yue and Loy 2024 ) can generate realistic facial details for severely degraded inputs, providing an effective balance between perceptual quality and restoration fidelity. Diffusion-prior-based methods, such as DiffBIR ( Lin et al. 2024 ) , OSDFace ( Wang et al. 2025 ) , and FiDeSR ( Kim et al. 2026 ) , rely on task-specific training, incurring substantial computational overhead. In contrast, posterior sampling methods ( Chung et al. 2023 ; Zheng et al. 2026 ) avoid retraining by incorporating degradation operators during reverse sampling. However, under severe degradations, the observed inputs often contain insufficient structural cues. This challenge is further exacerbated in real-world scenarios, where unknown degradation operators further prevent accurate degradation modeling and cause the reverse sampling trajectory to drift from the underlying facial structure. Therefore, for faithful face restoration, the key to posterior sampling is to effectively exploit limited observations to constrain reverse sampling. Wavelet-domain representations ( Mallat 1989 ) provide effective structural cues for face restoration by decomposing images into low- and high-frequency subbands ( Li et al. 2024 ) . The low-frequency subband preserves the coarse facial structure, while its Fourier phase ( Oppenheim and Lim 1981 ) encodes critical spatial information that remains relatively stable even under severe degradations. In contrast, the high-frequency subbands capture directional edges and fine facial textures, but their observed responses are often weak or unreliable. Consequently, insufficient low-frequency constraints can cause the restored face to deviate from the observed structure, whereas directly propagating or uniformly enhancing the observed high-frequency responses may amplify unreliable details. Therefore, low-frequency structures should remain aligned with the observations, while high-frequency details are better recovered through guided diffusion updates with additional controlled refinement of high-frequency information for severe degradations. Based on the above observations, we propose WaveFreqAnchor, a training-free diffusion framework for face restoration. Starting from a noised observation, it guides a frozen diffusion model through wave-structural anchoring and frequency correction. Anchor-Space Wave-Structural Guidance (ASWG) projects the predicted clean image to a low-resolution anchor space and enforces observation-consistent facial structures using pixel consistency and Laplacian-initialized anisotropic wave-response constraints. Multi-scale Wavelet-Fourier Injection (MWFI) preserves the predicted low-frequency amplitude, aligns its phase with the observation, and retains the guided high-frequency subbands. For synthetic super-resolution, the known degradation model provides an explicit low-resolution anchor, allowing the guided diffusion process to recover missing high-frequency details without additional refinement. For real-world restoration, where unknown degradations often leave facial details under-recovered, a frequency-ratio router adaptively selects the sampling configuration, and Subband High-Frequency Enhancement (SHE) performs bounded, spatially masked refinement on the predicted high-frequency subbands, while low-frequency correction is handled by MWFI. In summary, our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We proposed that ASWG imposes constraints on key facial structures and that MWFI corrects the low-frequency subbands in the facial predictions, thereby effectively constraining facial identity features. • For real-world degradations, we introduce a frequency-ratio routing scheme with input-dependent sampling configurations, and a SHE with bounded spatial masking to optimize the recovery of lost high-frequency details. • Experiments show that our method effectively improves the identity similarity of face restoration without training, particularly under severe degradation, while delivering excellent visual perceptual quality.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.text: Generative Priors for Face Restoration. Face restoration under severe degradation often relies on generative priors. PULSE ( Menon et al. 2020 ) searches the latent space of a pretrained GAN. Feed-forward methods incorporate generative facial priors ( Yang et al. 2021 ; Wang et al. 2021 ) , vector-quantized codebooks ( Gu et al. 2022 ; Zhou et al. 2022 ) , key-value priors ( Wang et al. 2022 ) , or prior-based latent transformations ( Xie et al. 2024 ) . Recent diffusion methods use a diffusion-based degradation remover followed by an enhancement module ( Wang et al. 2023c ) , combine a restoration module with diffusion-based generative refinement ( Lin et al. 2024 ) , bridge a restoration backbone to a pretrained diffusion prior through a transition distribution ( Yue and Loy 2024 ) , perform one-step restoration ( Wang et al. 2025 ) , or adapt the starting timestep and spatial guidance to estimated blur levels ( Do et al. 2025 ) . These methods rely on image-specific optimization or task-specific training. Our method instead guides a frozen face diffusion prior during inference without task-specific training. Diffusion Priors for Restoration. Pretrained diffusion priors have also been used for inverse restoration. DDRM ( Kawar et al. 2022 ) and DDNM ( Wang et al. 2023b ) enforce consistency under known linear operators. DPS ( Chung et al. 2023 ) guides reverse sampling with likelihood gradients. RED-Diff ( Mardani et al. 2024 ) formulates posterior inference through variational optimization, whereas P2L ( Chung et al. 2024 ) jointly optimizes prompt, latent, and pixel variables through alternating minimization. DAPS ( Zhang et al. 2025 ) uses decoupled noise annealing, and SubDAPS++ ( Zheng et al. 2026 ) extends it with dynamic-resolution diffusion priors. These methods generally assume a specified degradation operator and do not explicitly constrain observation-supported facial structure. PGDiff ( Yang et al. 2023 ) uses predefined image properties to guide pretrained diffusion priors, whereas SSDiff ( Li et al. 2025b ) constructs staged guidance from pseudo-references. PASDiff ( Ni et al. 2026 ) combines physics-aware photometric constraints with structural injection from an off-the-shelf face prior for low-light face restoration. In contrast, our method couples anchor-space wave-structural guidance with frequency-specific correction to keep reverse sampling tied to the facial structure supported by the observation. Frequency-Domain Restoration. Frequency-domain cues have been used in restoration objectives and model design. Focal Frequency Loss ( Jiang et al. 2021 ) emphasizes difficult spectral components during reconstruction, whereas Fourier space losses ( Fuoli et al. 2021 ) directly supervise frequency-domain discrepancies. WFEN ( Li et al. 2024 ) mitigates downsampling-induced feature distortion by decomposing facial features into low-frequency and high-frequency components. WaveFace ( Miao et al. 2024 ) applies diffusion to the low-frequency component and uses a separate network to recover high-frequency components. Recent diffusion methods use low- and high-frequency adaptive enhancers ( Kim et al. 2026 ) , wavelet-based high-frequency guidance ( Yang et al. 2026 ) , frequency-aligned self-distillation ( Choi et al. 2026 ) , or high-pass-filter-based diffusion guidance ( Li et al. 2026 ) . Given that Fourier phase carries spatial structure and high-frequency subbands encode local facial details, our method leverages these cues during reverse sampling by correcting the predicted low-frequency wavelet subband with the observation phase, preserving the high-frequency subbands from the guided update, and further refining them for real-world inputs, thereby maintaining observation-consistent structure and improving local detail recovery.

sections.heading: Sampling Framework
sections.text: Fig. 1 shows how the proposed corrections are incorporated into reverse sampling. ASWG computes the posterior gradient correction from the current clean estimate x ^ 0 | t \hat{x}_{0|t} . For real-world restoration, SHE additionally produces a refined estimate x ^ 0 | t ∗ \hat{x}_{0|t}^{*} . The refined estimate and the ASWG gradient are used in the guided posterior update, after which MWFI corrects the low-frequency wavelet subband while retaining the high-frequency subbands from x ~ t − 1 \tilde{x}_{t-1} . The same sampling formulation is used for synthetic and real-world inputs, with different anchor targets and sampling configurations. The known synthetic scale determines the anchor resolution, wavelet level, and associated parameters. For real-world inputs, a frequency-ratio router selects between two predefined configurations. After a light Gaussian prefilter, we compute the mean absolute magnitudes of the high-frequency wavelet coefficients at the first and third decomposition levels, denoted by E 1 E_{1} and E 3 E_{3} , and define r y = E 1 E 3 + ϵ . r_{y}=\frac{E_{1}}{E_{3}+\epsilon}. Inputs with r y < τ r r_{y}<\tau_{r} use the stronger configuration, and the remaining inputs use the milder configuration. The router contains no trainable component.

sections.heading: Subband High-Frequency Enhancement
sections.text: For synthetic SR, the known downsampling model provides an explicit LR anchor, so we rely on the guided diffusion update without an additional refinement branch. Under unknown real-world degradations, high-frequency facial details may remain under-recovered in the predicted clean image. As shown in the lower-right panel of Fig. 1 , SHE refines only its high-frequency wavelet subbands rather than sharpening the final image in pixel space. SHE leaves the low-frequency subband unchanged because MWFI corrects it separately. At timestep t t , we decompose the current clean estimate x ^ 0 | t \hat{x}_{0|t} by the same J J -level wavelet transform: ( L ​ L x ^ 0 | t , H x ^ 0 | t ) = DWT J ​ ( x ^ 0 | t ) , (LL_{\hat{x}_{0|t}},H_{\hat{x}_{0|t}})=\mathrm{DWT}_{J}(\hat{x}_{0|t}), (17) where H x ^ 0 | t = { H x ^ 0 | t j } j = 1 J H_{\hat{x}_{0|t}}=\{H_{\hat{x}_{0|t}}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{J} denotes the high-frequency subbands at different levels. For each level, we bound the high-frequency response to avoid amplifying unstable artifacts: H ¯ x ^ 0 | t j = clip ⁡ ( H x ^ 0 | t j , − k , k ) , \bar{H}_{\hat{x}_{0|t}}^{j}=\mathrm{clip}\left(H_{\hat{x}_{0|t}}^{j},-k,k\right), (18) where k > 0 k>0 is a fixed clipping threshold shared across wavelet levels. We then apply a controlled gain: H ~ x ^ 0 | t j = H x ^ 0 | t j + γ t ​ M j ⊙ H ¯ x ^ 0 | t j , \widetilde{H}_{\hat{x}_{0|t}}^{j}=H_{\hat{x}_{0|t}}^{j}+\gamma_{t}M^{j}\odot\bar{H}_{\hat{x}_{0|t}}^{j}, (19) where γ t \gamma_{t} is a boosting factor that is linearly reduced during the active refinement window, M j M^{j} is the spatial mask at level j j , and ⊙ \odot denotes the Hadamard product. This refinement strengthens local high-frequency details while leaving the low-frequency subband unchanged and introduces no additional generative prior.

Pipelines operating at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resize only the input internally, and their outputs are resized to 256 × 256 256\times 256 before evaluation. Synthetic metrics are PSNR, SSIM ( Wang et al. 2004 ) , LPIPS ( Zhang et al. 2018 ) , ID cosine similarity between Inception-ResNet embeddings pretrained on VGGFace2 ( Schroff et al. 2015 ; Cao et al. 2018 ) , and FAN landmark RMS distance ( Bulat and Tzimiropoulos 2017 ) . Real-world metrics are NIQE ( Mittal et al. 2013 ) , PI ( Blau et al. 2019 ) , MUSIQ ( Ke et al. 2021 ) , CLIPIQA ( Wang et al. 2023a ) , and TOPIQ ( Chen et al. 2024 ) . We use a 1000-step diffusion process with a linear noise schedule. For 4 × 4\times , 8 × 8\times , and 16 × 16\times synthetic SR, the starting timesteps are 500, 700, and 800. The anchor resolutions are 64 × 64 64\times 64 , 32 × 32 32\times 32 , and 16 × 16 16\times 16 , matching the true LR sizes, and the corresponding Haar wavelet levels are J = 2 , 3 , 4 J=2,3,4 . The guidance strengths are ( ζ , λ ) = ( 2.5 , 2.0 ) , ( 3.0 , 2.5 ) , ( 3.5 , 3.0 ) (\zeta,\lambda)=(2.5,2.0),(3.0,2.5),(3.5,3.0) , which are kept fixed during synthetic sampling. For real-world inputs, the frequency-ratio router selects the synthetic 8 × 8\times or 16 × 16\times parameter setting using τ r = 0.065 \tau_{r}=0.065 with linear annealing of the guidance strengths at late timesteps. Experiments run on an NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti (16GB) with PyTorch under Ubuntu 24.04.

sections.heading: Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods
sections.text: Table 1 compares synthetic FSR under 4 × 4\times , 8 × 8\times , and 16 × 16\times . At 4 × 4\times , our method ranks first on SSIM, LPIPS, ID, and LMD, and second on PSNR. At 8 × 8\times and 16 × 16\times , it obtains the best LPIPS, ID, and LMD. The advantages in identity similarity and landmark consistency remain evident under severe 16 × 16\times downsampling. The visual comparisons in Figure 2 show that our method can reconstruct faces with features that are closer to ground truth. Table 2 and Fig. 3 provide the quantitative and qualitative results on real-world scenes. Our method obtains the best results on all reported metrics across LFW-Test, WIDER-Test, and WebPhoto-Test, and achieves strong perceptual quality under real-world degradations.

sections.heading: Component contributions.
sections.text: The component ablation focuses on the severe 16 × 16\times setting, where identity-related structural drift is more evident. The last three rows of Table 3 show that ASWG improves identity similarity and landmark consistency over pixel-anchor-only guidance. Adding MWFI further improves both aspects. These results show that the two components progressively reduce identity-related structural drift under severe downsampling.

sections.heading: Definition of ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) .
sections.text: We examine the Laplacian initialization and direction-dependent propagation used in ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) . As shown in Table 4 , removing the Laplacian initialization improves identity similarity but weakens landmark consistency, whereas isotropic propagation slightly improves landmark consistency at the cost of identity similarity. The adopted Laplacian-initialized anisotropic form provides a better balance between identity similarity and landmark consistency.

sections.heading: Comparison with observation-guided methods.
sections.text: Table 3 also compares ASWG with representative observation-guided diffusion methods. ASWG achieves the best landmark consistency among the compared methods while maintaining competitive identity similarity, showing that its structural guidance more reliably preserves facial geometry.

sections.heading: Low-frequency correction.
sections.text: At each timestep in the active MWFI window, we compare the LL-only reconstructions before and after phase correction with their ground-truth counterparts using PSNR, LPIPS, and DISTS ( Ding et al. 2022 ) , with all high-frequency subbands set to zero. As shown in Table 5 , phase correction improves both the pixel fidelity and perceptual similarity of the low-frequency reconstruction. Fig. 4 further shows that MWFI better aligns the overall facial shape and the relative positions of facial components with the ground truth in the final output.

sections.heading: High-frequency enhancement.
sections.text: Because SHE targets high-frequency facial details that may remain under-recovered in real-world inputs, we evaluate it by disabling the high-frequency subband refinement. As shown in Table 6 , SHE improves the overall no-reference perceptual quality of real-world restoration. Fig. 5 further shows clearer eyeglass frames, hair boundaries, and local facial contours, supporting its ability to recover high-frequency facial details.

sections.heading: Adaptive configuration.
sections.text: A single sampling configuration is not suitable for all real-world inputs. As shown in Fig. 6 , the 16 × 16\times preset produces clearer facial components when fine-scale cues are weak. When more usable cues remain, the 8 × 8\times preset better retains the input-supported facial appearance, whereas the 16 × 16\times preset produces more pronounced changes in local facial characteristics. The frequency-ratio router therefore selects between the two predefined configurations according to r y r_{y} .

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: For our method, severe color casts, over-exposure, and low facial contrast also remain challenging. The two-configuration router cannot fully cover the continuous range of real degradations. Future work will explore robust identity-related constraints and degradation-aware parameter selection.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: We proposed WaveFreqAnchor, a training-free framework that improves diffusion-based face restoration through wave-structural anchoring and frequency-guided correction. By jointly introducing ASWG, MWFI, and SHE, our method effectively mitigates structural drift while preserving facial identity and recovering realistic high-frequency details under severe real-world degradations. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of combining wavelet-domain structural guidance with frequency-aware diffusion for high-fidelity face restoration.

Abstract Diffusion-based face restoration that adjusts the sampling trajectory of pre-trained diffusion models has achieved remarkable progress. However, existing approaches provide insufficient constraints during reverse diffusion, causing identity-related structural drift and degraded fidelity under severe degradations. To address this, we propose WaveFreqAnchor, a training-free framework based on Wave-Structural Anchoring and Frequency Correction Diffusion. Specifically, Anchor-Space Wave-Structural Guidance (ASWG) constrains facial structures through anisotropic wave-response consistency, while Multi-scale Wavelet-Fourier Injection (MWFI) aligns the predicted low-frequency subband with the observation by replacing its phase, correcting inconsistencies accumulated during reverse diffusion. For real-world scenes, we further introduce Subband High-Frequency Enhancement (SHE), which performs bounded, spatially masked refinement on the predicted high-frequency subbands to recover fine facial details under unknown compound degradations. Together, these designs effectively preserve facial identity while restoring sharp and realistic facial details. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving high-quality and high-fidelity face restoration. 1 Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications 2 Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications 3 Nanjing University of Science and Technology 4 East China Normal University {klive0417, lewj2408}@gmail.com, {zxwang, gwgao}@njust.edu.cn, jcli@cs.ecnu.edu.cn, wangcl@njupt.edu.cn Introduction Figure 1: Overview of our WaveFreqAnchor. Given the input observation, ASWG provides gradient guidance for posterior sampling, while MWFI corrects the predicted low-frequency wavelet subband using the observed phase and preserves the high-frequency subbands from the guided update. For real-world inputs with missing high-frequency details, SHE further refines the predicted high-frequency subbands before the posterior update. Face restoration ( Li et al. 2025a ) aims to recover a high-quality face image from a degraded input. Under severe degradations, only coarse facial structures and limited identity cues remain, making the restoration problem highly ill-posed and often leading to plausible yet identity-inconsistent results. Existing methods leverage generative facial priors ( Wang et al. 2021 ) , discrete codebooks ( Zhou et al. 2022 ) , and diffusion priors ( Lin et al. 2024 ; Wang et al. 2025 ) to constrain the solution space. However, even when producing visually realistic results, they often fail to faithfully preserve the observed facial structures under severe degradations. Achieving both realistic detail synthesis and structural fidelity therefore remains a fundamental challenge. Pre-trained diffusion models ( Yue and Loy 2024 ) can generate realistic facial details for severely degraded inputs, providing an effective balance between perceptual quality and restoration fidelity. Diffusion-prior-based methods, such as DiffBIR ( Lin et al. 2024 ) , OSDFace ( Wang et al. 2025 ) , and FiDeSR ( Kim et al. 2026 ) , rely on task-specific training, incurring substantial computational overhead. In contrast, posterior sampling methods ( Chung et al. 2023 ; Zheng et al. 2026 ) avoid retraining by incorporating degradation operators during reverse sampling. However, under severe degradations, the observed inputs often contain insufficient structural cues. This challenge is further exacerbated in real-world scenarios, where unknown degradation operators further prevent accurate degradation modeling and cause the reverse sampling trajectory to drift from the underlying facial structure. Therefore, for faithful face restoration, the key to posterior sampling is to effectively exploit limited observations to constrain reverse sampling. Wavelet-domain representations ( Mallat 1989 ) provide effective structural cues for face restoration by decomposing images into low- and high-frequency subbands ( Li et al. 2024 ) . The low-frequency subband preserves the coarse facial structure, while its Fourier phase ( Oppenheim and Lim 1981 ) encodes critical spatial information that remains relatively stable even under severe degradations. In contrast, the high-frequency subbands capture directional edges and fine facial textures, but their observed responses are often weak or unreliable. Consequently, insufficient low-frequency constraints can cause the restored face to deviate from the observed structure, whereas directly propagating or uniformly enhancing the observed high-frequency responses may amplify unreliable details. Therefore, low-frequency structures should remain aligned with the observations, while high-frequency details are better recovered through guided diffusion updates with additional controlled refinement of high-frequency information for severe degradations. Based on the above observations, we propose WaveFreqAnchor, a training-free diffusion framework for face restoration. Starting from a noised observation, it guides a frozen diffusion model through wave-structural anchoring and frequency correction. Anchor-Space Wave-Structural Guidance (ASWG) projects the predicted clean image to a low-resolution anchor space and enforces observation-consistent facial structures using pixel consistency and Laplacian-initialized anisotropic wave-response constraints. Multi-scale Wavelet-Fourier Injection (MWFI) preserves the predicted low-frequency amplitude, aligns its phase with the observation, and retains the guided high-frequency subbands. For synthetic super-resolution, the known degradation model provides an explicit low-resolution anchor, allowing the guided diffusion process to recover missing high-frequency details without additional refinement. For real-world restoration, where unknown degradations often leave facial details under-recovered, a frequency-ratio router adaptively selects the sampling configuration, and Subband High-Frequency Enhancement (SHE) performs bounded, spatially masked refinement on the predicted high-frequency subbands, while low-frequency correction is handled by MWFI. In summary, our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We proposed that ASWG imposes constraints on key facial structures and that MWFI corrects the low-frequency subbands in the facial predictions, thereby effectively constraining facial identity features. • For real-world degradations, we introduce a frequency-ratio routing scheme with input-dependent sampling configurations, and a SHE with bounded spatial masking to optimize the recovery of lost high-frequency details. • Experiments show that our method effectively improves the identity similarity of face restoration without training, particularly under severe degradation, while delivering excellent visual perceptual quality. Related Work Generative Priors for Face Restoration. Face restoration under severe degradation often relies on generative priors. PULSE ( Menon et al. 2020 ) searches the latent space of a pretrained GAN. Feed-forward methods incorporate generative facial priors ( Yang et al. 2021 ; Wang et al. 2021 ) , vector-quantized codebooks ( Gu et al. 2022 ; Zhou et al. 2022 ) , key-value priors ( Wang et al. 2022 ) , or prior-based latent transformations ( Xie et al. 2024 ) . Recent diffusion methods use a diffusion-based degradation remover followed by an enhancement module ( Wang et al. 2023c ) , combine a restoration module with diffusion-based generative refinement ( Lin et al. 2024 ) , bridge a restoration backbone to a pretrained diffusion prior through a transition distribution ( Yue and Loy 2024 ) , perform one-step restoration ( Wang et al. 2025 ) , or adapt the starting timestep and spatial guidance to estimated blur levels ( Do et al. 2025 ) . These methods rely on image-specific optimization or task-specific training. Our method instead guides a frozen face diffusion prior during inference without task-specific training. Diffusion Priors for Restoration. Pretrained diffusion priors have also been used for inverse restoration. DDRM ( Kawar et al. 2022 ) and DDNM ( Wang et al. 2023b ) enforce consistency under known linear operators. DPS ( Chung et al. 2023 ) guides reverse sampling with likelihood gradients. RED-Diff ( Mardani et al. 2024 ) formulates posterior inference through variational optimization, whereas P2L ( Chung et al. 2024 ) jointly optimizes prompt, latent, and pixel variables through alternating minimization. DAPS ( Zhang et al. 2025 ) uses decoupled noise annealing, and SubDAPS++ ( Zheng et al. 2026 ) extends it with dynamic-resolution diffusion priors. These methods generally assume a specified degradation operator and do not explicitly constrain observation-supported facial structure. PGDiff ( Yang et al. 2023 ) uses predefined image properties to guide pretrained diffusion priors, whereas SSDiff ( Li et al. 2025b ) constructs staged guidance from pseudo-references. PASDiff ( Ni et al. 2026 ) combines physics-aware photometric constraints with structural injection from an off-the-shelf face prior for low-light face restoration. In contrast, our method couples anchor-space wave-structural guidance with frequency-specific correction to keep reverse sampling tied to the facial structure supported by the observation. Frequency-Domain Restoration. Frequency-domain cues have been used in restoration objectives and model design. Focal Frequency Loss ( Jiang et al. 2021 ) emphasizes difficult spectral components during reconstruction, whereas Fourier space losses ( Fuoli et al. 2021 ) directly supervise frequency-domain discrepancies. WFEN ( Li et al. 2024 ) mitigates downsampling-induced feature distortion by decomposing facial features into low-frequency and high-frequency components. WaveFace ( Miao et al. 2024 ) applies diffusion to the low-frequency component and uses a separate network to recover high-frequency components. Recent diffusion methods use low- and high-frequency adaptive enhancers ( Kim et al. 2026 ) , wavelet-based high-frequency guidance ( Yang et al. 2026 ) , frequency-aligned self-distillation ( Choi et al. 2026 ) , or high-pass-filter-based diffusion guidance ( Li et al. 2026 ) . Given that Fourier phase carries spatial structure and high-frequency subbands encode local facial details, our method leverages these cues during reverse sampling by correcting the predicted low-frequency wavelet subband with the observation phase, preserving the high-frequency subbands from the guided update, and further refining them for real-world inputs, thereby maintaining observation-consistent structure and improving local detail recovery. Methods Problem Formulation and Diffusion Prior Let y y denote the aligned and resized degraded face observation. Our method restores y y with a frozen diffusion prior ( Ho et al. 2020 ) , without task-specific training. Because SHE targets high-frequency facial details that may remain under-recovered in real-world inputs, we evaluate it by disabling the high-frequency subband refinement. A single sampling configuration is not suitable for all real-world inputs. As shown in Fig. 6 , the 16 × 16	imes preset produces clearer facial components when fine-scale cues are weak. Limitations and Future Work For our method, severe color casts, over-exposure, and low facial contrast also remain challenging. The two-configuration router cannot fully cover the continuous range of real degradations. Future work will explore robust identity-related constraints and degradation-aware parameter selection. Conclusion We proposed WaveFreqAnchor, a training-free framework that improves diffusion-based face restoration through wave-structural anchoring and frequency-guided correction. By jointly introducing ASWG, MWFI, and SHE, our method effectively mitigates structural drift while preserving facial identity and recovering realistic high-frequency details under severe real-world degradations. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of combining wavelet-domain structural guidance with frequency-aware diffusion for high-fidelity face restoration.
